claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries cause local stress concentrations in the untreated alloy.
The local stress concentrations caused by dislocation pile-ups promote microcracking and catastrophic or brittle failure during room-temperature tensile loading.
A thin, ductile interphase can be incorporated at the lamellar interfaces.
Targeted heat treatment can produce the proposed interfacial modification.
Localized alloying that changes internal-boundary chemistry can produce the proposed interfacial modification.
The ductile interphase will facilitate smoother dislocation transmission between the constituent phases.
The ductile interphase will reduce dislocation accumulation at lamellar boundaries.
Reduced dislocation accumulation will lower local stress concentrations.
The interphase will distribute plastic deformation more uniformly.
More uniform plastic deformation and lower stress localization will delay microcrack initiation.
The intervention can retain the dual-phase morphology associated with high strength.
The modified alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The modified alloy will retain or potentially increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Preservation of the dual-phase architecture is necessary to retain high strength.
An excessively thick or extensive ductile interphase may reduce strength.
The proposed effects are intended to apply under room-temperature tensile loading and may not extend to high-temperature or other operating regimes.
